content: Pain following a caesarean section can significantly impact a mother’s physical and emotional well-being, as well as her ability to care for her newborn. Conventional pain management strategies are often underutilized due to concerns about potential adverse effects on both the mother and the neonate. Complementary and alternative medicine (CAM) therapies have been proposed as potential options for managing post-caesarean pain. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of CAM therapies in alleviating post-caesarean pain. A comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth’s Trials Register, LILACS, PEDro, CAMbase, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, up to September 6, 2019. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs), including quasi-RCTs and cluster-RCTs, were included if they compared CAM therapies (alone or in combination with other pain relief methods) to other treatments, placebo, or no treatment. A total of 37 studies involving 3,076 women were included, investigating eight different CAM therapies. However, the trials exhibited substantial heterogeneity, and the certainty of evidence was downgraded due to small sample sizes, risk of bias, lack of blinding, and inadequate reporting of randomization processes. None of the trials assessed pain outcomes at six weeks post-discharge. The primary outcomes were pain and adverse effects, while secondary outcomes included vital signs and the need for rescue analgesics at six weeks, though these were poorly reported or not reported at all. Acupuncture or Acupressure The evidence regarding the effects of acupuncture or acupressure on post-caesarean pain is of very low certainty. It is unclear whether acupuncture or acupressure alone, or in combination with analgesia, reduces pain compared to no treatment or placebo. However, acupuncture or acupressure combined with analgesia may reduce pain at 12 hours (SMD -0.28, 95% CI -0.64 to 0.07; 2 studies, 130 women) and 24 hours (SMD -0.63, 95% CI -0.99 to -0.26; 2 studies, 130 women), though the evidence is of low certainty. The impact of acupuncture or acupressure on adverse effects remains uncertain due to the very low quality of evidence. Aromatherapy Aromatherapy combined with analgesia may reduce pain compared to placebo plus analgesia at 12 hours (MD -2.63 on a visual analogue scale [VAS], 95% CI -3.48 to -1.77; 3 studies, 360 women) and 24 hours (MD -3.38 VAS, 95% CI -3.85 to -2.91; 1 study, 200 women). However, the evidence is of low certainty. The effect of aromatherapy on adverse effects, such as anxiety, is uncertain. Electromagnetic Therapy Electromagnetic therapy may reduce pain compared to placebo plus analgesia at 12 hours (MD -8.00 VAS, 95% CI -11.65 to -4.35; 1 study, 72 women) and 24 hours (MD -13.00 VAS, 95% CI -17.13 to -8.87; 1 study, 72 women). The evidence supporting these findings is of low certainty. Massage Six studies (651 women) evaluated the effects of massage (foot and hand) combined with analgesia compared to analgesia alone. Five of these studies were quasi-RCTs. The evidence regarding pain relief, adverse effects (e.g., anxiety), vital signs, and the need for rescue analgesics was of very low certainty. Music Therapy Music therapy combined with analgesia may reduce pain compared to placebo plus analgesia at one hour (SMD -0.84, 95% CI -1.23 to -0.46; 2 studies, 115 women) and 24 hours (MD -1.79, 95% CI -2.67 to -0.91; 1 study, 38 women). Music therapy may also reduce pain compared to analgesia alone at one hour (MD -2.11, 95% CI -3.11 to -1.10; 1 study, 38 women) and 24 hours (MD -2.69, 95% CI -3.67 to -1.70; 1 study, 38 women). However, the evidence is of low certainty. The effect of music therapy on adverse effects, such as anxiety, is uncertain due to very low-quality evidence. Reiki The effects of Reiki combined with analgesia compared to analgesia alone on pain, adverse effects, vital signs, or the need for rescue analgesics are uncertain due to very low-quality evidence (1 study, 90 women). Relaxation Techniques Relaxation techniques may reduce pain compared to standard care at 24 hours (MD -0.53 VAS, 95% CI -1.05 to -0.01; 1 study, 60 women). The evidence supporting this finding is of low certainty. Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation (TENS) TENS may reduce pain compared to no treatment at one hour (MD -2.26 VAS, 95% CI -3.35 to -1.17; 1 study, 40 women). TENS combined with analgesia may reduce pain compared to placebo plus analgesia at one hour (SMD -1.10 VAS, 95% CI -1.37 to -0.82; 3 studies, 238 women) and 24 hours (MD -0.70 VAS, 95% CI -0.87 to -0.53; 1 study, 108 women). TENS combined with analgesia may also reduce heart rate (MD -7.00 bpm, 95% CI -7.63 to -6.37; 1 study, 108 women) and respiratory rate (MD -1.10 breaths per minute, 95% CI -1.26 to -0.94; 1 study, 108 women). However, the effects of TENS on pain at six hours or 24 hours, as well as on vital signs, remain uncertain due to very low-quality evidence (2 studies, 92 women). Authors' Conclusions Some CAM therapies may provide short-term pain relief (up to 24 hours) following a caesarean section. However, the evidence regarding adverse effects is too uncertain to draw conclusions about safety, and there is no evidence on the long-term effects of these therapies. Future research should prioritize pain as a primary outcome, measured as the proportion of participants achieving at least moderate (30%) or substantial (50%) pain relief. Using dichotomous pain outcomes would enhance the clarity and applicability of findings. Additionally, future trials should be adequately powered to detect clinically meaningful effects, assess other important outcomes, and utilize validated measurement tools.
